A code review is a sampling process, not an exhaustive one. Reviewers check a diff against the patterns of bugs they know to look for — null checks, off-by-ones, race conditions, obvious logic errors — in the time they have. A clean pass means "the reviewer didn't spot a problem with the techniques they applied," which is a much narrower claim than "no problem exists."

Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence here because the review's coverage is unknown and usually partial. A reviewer skimming a 500-line diff in fifteen minutes has a different false-negative rate than one who traced every call path. Correctness bugs also hide in places review is structurally bad at reaching: concurrency timing, edge-case inputs never considered, integration behavior across services, performance under load. Review catches what pattern-matches against known failure modes; novel or environment-dependent bugs slip straight through.

There's also a selection effect: what gets reviewed is what's visible in the diff. Bugs caused by an interaction between the new code and existing code the reviewer didn't re-check, or by an assumption baked into a part of the system the diff doesn't touch, are invisible to that lens no matter how careful the reviewer is.

Practically: treat a clean review as "no found defects of the kind this review could find," and keep tests, static analysis, and runtime observation as the actual evidence of correctness. Review is one layer that reduces risk, not a proof.

A clean code review is evidence of absence, not absence of evidence. Reviewers catch what they know to look for and what the diff makes visible; they miss bugs in logic paths nobody traced, edge cases nobody tried, and interactions with code outside the diff. Silence means "no reviewer flagged anything," not "no defect exists" — those are different claims, and treating them as the same is the error.

Reviews are also bounded by attention and framing. A reviewer skimming a large diff, unfamiliar with the domain, or primed by the PR description to look for one kind of problem will systematically miss others. Two reviewers can each find nothing and still have covered different 80% slices of the risk — their silence doesn't compose into full coverage.

Review catches a different class of bug than testing does: naming, structure, missed conventions, obvious logic errors visible from reading. It does not execute the code. Concurrency bugs, off-by-ones under specific inputs, integration failures with real data, performance cliffs — these routinely survive review and only surface at runtime or under test. So "reviewed, nothing found" answers "did a human reading it spot a problem," not "does this behave correctly."

Correctness needs corroborating evidence: tests that exercise the actual behavior, runtime checks, or production signal — not another round of reading. Treat a clean review as one data point that lowers risk, never as the proof that closes the question.

A code review's absence of findings is bounded by what the reviewer actually checked, not by what's true of the code. A human reviewer reads a diff and reasons about the paths they can hold in mind — the happy path, maybe one or two edge cases they think to consider. Concurrency bugs, off-by-one errors triggered only at specific input sizes, integration failures that only surface when this code meets a caller three modules away — none of these announce themselves to a reader scanning a diff. Silence means "I found no problems," not "there are no problems."

Review also targets a narrow slice of what makes code correct. Reviewers check for style violations, obvious logic errors, and adherence to conventions — but rarely trace every runtime value through every branch, which is what actual correctness requires. A function can pass review because it reads cleanly and still crash on empty input, because no one traced that specific case by hand.

Absence of comments can also reflect reviewer fatigue, unfamiliarity with the subsystem, or a shallow pass rather than a thorough one. A reviewer skimming a 500-line diff on a Friday afternoon produces the same "looks good" output as one who traced every branch — the review artifact doesn't distinguish rigor from rubber-stamping.

None of this means review is worthless — it catches real classes of bugs cheaply. It means clean review results are one input, not proof. Correctness claims need tests, types, and runtime verification alongside review; treat "reviewed, no findings" as "no bugs found this way," not "no bugs."

A code review is a search over a hypothesis space, not a proof. Reviewers check for the bug patterns they know to look for — off-by-ones, missing null checks, race conditions, wrong operator precedence — against the mental model they've built of what the code does. A silent finish means none of those specific checks fired, not that the space of possible defects is empty. The reviewer's attention, experience and time are all finite; a clean pass reflects the coverage of the review, not the code.

The mental model itself can be wrong in ways that make bugs invisible. If a reviewer misreads what a function does, they'll judge the code correct relative to their misunderstanding, and the review will pass while the actual behavior stays broken. This is why two reviewers using different mental models can both give a clean pass to code that's still buggy — each review is only as strong as the model behind it, and a shared blind spot produces a shared false negative.

Review also can't catch what it never exercises. Static reading misses issues that only appear under real inputs, timing, concurrency, or scale — a race condition, a memory leak under load, a subtle numerical error. Tests, fuzzing and production monitoring probe axes a review by inspection doesn't reach, which is why "reviewed" and "verified" are different claims.

None of this makes review worthless — it catches a real, useful class of defects cheaply. But treat a clean review as "no known-pattern bugs found by this reviewer's model," not "no bugs." Pair it with tests, adversarial review from someone with a different mental model, and runtime signal before calling something correct.

A finding of "nothing wrong" only tells you the reviewer didn't spot a problem in the time they spent — it says nothing about whether a problem exists. Review is bounded by what the reviewer thought to check, the paths they traced, and the inputs they imagined. Bugs that live outside that scope (a race condition, an edge case with empty input, a wrong assumption both author and reviewer share) are invisible to the process by construction, not by chance.

This is why review complements tests and doesn't replace them. Tests execute the code against concrete inputs and check actual behavior; review is a human reading code and predicting behavior. Prediction is fallible in ways execution isn't — a reviewer can misread a boundary condition, miss that two functions interact badly three files apart, or simply get tired on a long diff. A clean review plus a passing test suite is stronger evidence than either alone, but even that combination only covers the cases someone thought to write.

There's also a shared-blind-spot problem specific to review. If the author made an assumption that's wrong, the reviewer often shares the same mental model — that's usually *why* they didn't catch it. A second pair of eyes helps most when it's a genuinely different pair of eyes: someone who knows the domain differently, or who deliberately tries to break the code rather than confirm it works.

Practically: treat "review found nothing" as "no *known* problems," not "no problems." Keep pushing on other evidence — tests, especially edge cases; runtime checks; monitoring after deploy. The absence of a finding is the absence of a finding, not a proof of correctness.

Absence of findings only proves review didn't surface anything — it doesn't prove nothing is there. Correctness is a claim about all inputs and all execution paths; a reviewer inspects a finite slice of that space, bounded by what they read, understood, and thought to check. A clean pass reflects the reviewer's attention and the bugs they know to look for, not the code's actual behavior across every path.

Reviews also aren't exhaustive by design — reviewers skim familiar patterns, trust code that "looks right," and rarely trace every branch, concurrency interleaving, or edge case by hand. Bugs that only manifest under specific inputs, timing, or scale routinely survive review because nobody exercised that path mentally. This is why review complements tests and doesn't replace them: tests execute the code and check actual behavior, while review checks whether the code matches the reviewer's mental model of intended behavior — two different, both incomplete, signals.

Treat a clean review as "no objections raised," not "verified correct." Correctness claims should rest on evidence that exercises the code — tests, runtime checks, verified specs — not on the silence of a manual read.

A code review's power is bounded by what its reviewers know to look for and how the code is exercised. A reviewer reads the diff, reasons about intended behavior, and checks it against experience — but that process only catches classes of bugs the reviewer has seen before or can spot by inspection. Concurrency races, edge cases in rarely-hit input ranges, integration failures with systems the reviewer isn't familiar with, and performance regressions under load are all invisible to a human reading a diff, no matter how careful.

Absence of findings is also just as easily explained by reviewer fatigue, unfamiliarity with the subsystem, or a diff too large to hold in working memory as by the code being flawless. A rushed 500-line review and a careful 20-line review both end in "no comments" but carry very different confidence.

Review and testing check different things: review checks whether the code's logic matches intent; tests and runtime checks whether the code's behavior matches reality. A clean review with no tests run, no execution against real inputs, and no verification of the actual feature working is a claim about legibility, not correctness.

Treat "review passed" as one data point, not a proof. Pair it with running the tests, exercising the golden path and edge cases yourself, and — for anything security- or correctness-critical — an adversarial second look that's actively trying to break the code rather than confirm it works.

A code review checks a fixed set of hypotheses the reviewer thought to check — naming, obvious edge cases, common bug patterns, style. It does not check hypotheses nobody raised. Silence means "the reviewer found no problems among the things they looked for," not "no problems exist." A defect outside the reviewer's mental model — a race condition, a wrong assumption baked into a requirement, a subtle off-by-one triggered only by production data shapes — produces the same clean report as genuinely correct code, because both leave zero traces in the reviewer's search space.

This is compounded by the fact that review is a static, human read-through, not an execution. Reviewers simulate code in their head, and that simulation is unreliable for anything with real state, concurrency, or many input branches. Tests, fuzzing, and running the code exercise actual execution paths; review exercises the reviewer's mental model of those paths, which routinely diverges from what the interpreter or compiler will actually do.

Review is also biased toward what's visible in the diff. Bugs from missing cases (an unhandled branch that was never written, an authorization check that was never added) are invisible to a reviewer scanning what's there — you can't spot the absence of a check as easily as a bug in a check that exists. And familiarity works against thoroughness: the more a reviewer trusts an author or a well-trodden code path, the shallower the read, so "reviewed and approved" often correlates more with reviewer trust than with code correctness.

Practical implication: treat a clean review as one data point, not a proof. Pair it with tests that actually execute the code, and where possible, with someone or something actively trying to break the code (adversarial review, fuzzing) rather than only confirming it looks right.

A code review finding nothing tests only for the specific bugs the reviewer knew to look for. Absence of findings measures reviewer coverage, not code correctness — a review scans a fixed set of patterns (common mistakes, style violations, familiar failure modes) against the code. Bugs outside that pattern set produce no signal at all, so "nothing found" and "nothing wrong" are different claims that happen to look identical in the output.

Three specific gaps this misses. Novel bugs: logic errors that don't match any pattern the reviewer has seen before slip through regardless of reviewer skill. Runtime-only failures: race conditions, off-by-one errors under specific data, and integration failures between correctly-written pieces are often invisible from reading code alone — they require execution. Blind spots by construction: a reviewer who misunderstands the requirement will approve code that correctly implements the wrong thing, since the review checks the code against the reviewer's mental model, not against reality.

This is why review complements testing rather than replacing it — a clean review plus passing tests is stronger evidence than either alone, because they fail differently. Tests exercise actual behavior against expected outputs; review checks structure and intent a test suite might not cover (readability, security patterns, edge-case reasoning). Treat "no findings" as "no known problems found," not "verified correct," and keep pushing on execution-based verification (tests, staging runs, monitoring) even after a review comes back clean.

A code review checks for defects the reviewer knows to look for — it's a search over a hypothesis space bounded by the reviewer's experience, attention, and the time given. A clean pass means none of the checked hypotheses turned up a match; it says nothing about defects outside that space. Race conditions, off-by-ones under rare inputs, integration failures with systems not in view, and misunderstood requirements routinely survive review specifically because they don't look wrong on the page.

Review is also static: the reviewer reads code and reasons about behavior, but doesn't execute it against real data, real load, or real concurrency. Correctness is a claim about runtime behavior across all reachable states; a review samples none of that directly. Two additional gaps compound this: reviewers anchor on the diff's intent and check "does this do what the author meant," not "does this handle every input," and reviewer fatigue or unfamiliarity with a subsystem silently shrinks the search space without any signal that it shrank.

None of this makes review useless — it catches classes of bugs testing doesn't (design flaws, unclear intent, missed edge cases a test suite never conceived of). But "reviewed, no issues found" and "verified correct" are different claims. The first is bounded by what was checked; the second requires tests, execution, and evidence. Treat a clean review as one filter passed, not a certificate — pair it with tests, and stay suspicious of any path the review didn't actually exercise.

Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. A review checks specific properties a reviewer thought to check — naming, obvious edge cases, matching the diff against the ticket. Bugs outside that lens (concurrency races, a wrong assumption baked into the design, an edge case nobody imagined) leave no trace for a clean review to find. "Nothing found" describes the reviewer's search, not the code's correctness.

Review is also bounded by what the reviewer can hold in their head at once. A diff reads locally — line by line, function by function — while real bugs often live in the gaps: how this change interacts with a caller three files away, a state mutation that only breaks under a specific ordering, a test that passes because it never exercises the changed path. Static reading catches typos and logic slips; it doesn't run the code.

Tests, type checks, and execution find a different class of defect than review does — they check *what happens*, not *what looks right*. A function can read correctly and still crash on the input nobody typed into the diff. Treat "review passed" as "no reviewer-visible red flags," not "verified correct" — the latter needs execution: run it, test it, watch it handle the edge cases.

Practically: a clean review lowers risk, it doesn't zero it out. Pair it with running the code — the golden path and the edge cases — before calling anything done.

A code review checks whether the reviewer noticed problems, not whether the code is correct — those are different claims. Reviewers read a diff against their own mental model, which has blind spots: unfamiliar edge cases, assumptions about caller behavior, race conditions that only show up under concurrency. "I didn't see a bug" reports the search, not the target.

Absence of findings correlates with what the review covered, not with correctness. A review scoped to style and structure won't surface a logic bug; a reviewer unfamiliar with the domain won't catch a subtle spec violation. Coverage gaps are invisible from outside the review — a clean report looks identical whether the code was scrutinized deeply or skimmed.

Correctness is an empirical property: does the code behave right across the actual input space and environment. Review is static and human-paced; it can't execute concurrent paths, adversarial inputs, or production load. Tests, types, and runtime observation catch categories of bugs review structurally cannot — that's why they're complementary, not redundant.

Treat a clean review as "no known issues so far," not "verified correct." Pair it with tests, and stay alert for the specific failure modes review is weakest against — concurrency, edge-case inputs, integration behavior.

A code review's absence of findings is bounded by what the reviewer actually checked, not by what's true of the code. Reviewers work from a mental model of expected behavior, common bug patterns, and the diff in front of them — they don't execute every path or enumerate every input. A bug that falls outside that model (an edge case never considered, an interaction with a module not in the diff, a timing issue that only surfaces under load) simply won't register as a finding, because the reviewer never looked in that direction. Silence means "nothing wrong turned up in the places I checked," not "nothing is wrong."

This is also a statement about absence of evidence. Finding zero bugs is consistent with two very different worlds: one where the code is correct, and one where the code has bugs the review's method can't surface — wrong test doubles, missing negative-path checks, a reviewer unfamiliar with the domain, time pressure that limited depth. A clean review can't distinguish between these worlds, so it can't be used as proof of the first one.

Compounding this, review quality itself varies and is rarely visible from the output. A thorough review and a rushed skim can both end in "LGTM," but they carry very different amounts of evidence. Without knowing what was actually exercised — which files were read closely, which edge cases were considered, whether the reviewer ran the code or just read it — a clean result tells you almost nothing about how hard anyone looked.

Practical implication: treat "review passed" as one weak signal among several, not a correctness proof. Pair it with tests that actually execute the code, type checking, and — for anything with real risk — actually running the feature. Correctness claims need evidence that was exercised, not evidence that was merely absent.

A code review checking "does this look right" only tests against reviewers' assumptions and known bug patterns — it can't exercise the code. It doesn't run the paths that trigger under specific inputs, timing, or state, so bugs outside the reviewers' mental model pass silently.

Correctness claims need evidence from execution: tests, types, runtime checks. Review catches things execution doesn't (design flaws, missed edge cases, unclear intent) — but it's a different failure mode than execution testing, not a stronger one. Passing review and passing tests together are still just two more failure modes surviving, not proof of correctness.

Absence of findings is often absence of scrutiny, not absence of bugs — reviewer fatigue, unfamiliarity with the code, or a shallow pass all produce "looks fine" with no correlation to actual correctness. Treat a clean review as "no issues surfaced by this pass," not "verified correct," and pair it with tests before trusting the code.

A code review checks for the presence of visible defects, not the absence of all defects. Reviewers scan the diff for what they recognize as wrong — familiar bug patterns, style violations, obvious logic errors. A clean scan means none of those familiar patterns matched; it says nothing about failure modes the reviewer didn't think to look for, code paths they didn't trace, or interactions with the rest of the system they didn't have context on. Absence of a finding is a property of the search, not the code.

This is asymmetric evidence: a review that flags a real bug gives you strong, verifiable proof (you can reproduce it), but a review that flags nothing gives you almost no proof of correctness. It's the same logical gap as "no evidence of X" versus "evidence of no X" — a review's silence just means the specific checks it ran passed, out of the near-infinite set of checks that could have run.

Reviews are also bounded by human attention and time. A reviewer skims a diff in minutes; they don't execute every branch, don't check every edge case against the spec, and rarely have the full runtime context (concurrent access, real data shapes, downstream consumers) that would surface a subtler bug. Concurrency bugs, off-by-one errors under rare inputs, and integration mismatches routinely survive multiple clean reviews and only surface under production load or targeted testing.

So treat a clean review as "no known-pattern defects found," not "verified correct." Correctness comes from tests, type checks, runtime verification, and tracing actual behavior against the spec — the review is one filter among several, not the proof itself.

A code review is a sample of checks, not an exhaustive proof. Reviewers look for patterns they recognize — known bug shapes, style violations, obvious logic errors — within the time they have. Bugs outside that pattern library, or ones requiring deep tracing through runtime state, concurrency timing, or business-logic edge cases, simply don't surface through visual inspection. "No comments" means "nothing matched what the reviewer was primed to catch," not "nothing is wrong."

Absence of evidence is weak evidence of absence only when the search method has high coverage. Code review doesn't: it's bounded by the reviewer's familiarity with the domain, the size of the diff, fatigue, and what got prioritized in a fixed time slot. A reviewer skimming a 500-line PR in 15 minutes has fundamentally different coverage than one who traced every call site. Neither produces a false "not correct" signal — they just don't produce a true "correct" signal either.

This is also why review and testing are complementary, not redundant. Review catches things tests don't (design flaws, unclear intent, missing edge-case handling that no one thought to test for). Tests catch things review doesn't (actual runtime behavior, integration failures, regressions). A clean review plus a green test suite is much stronger evidence than either alone — but even that combination only proves the code behaves correctly for the inputs and conditions actually exercised.

Practically: treat "review found nothing" as "no known-bad pattern was spotted," and keep the actual correctness signal — tests, types, runtime verification — as the real bar. Don't let a quiet review lower your guard on verifying the change actually works.

A clean review is evidence the reviewer found nothing, not evidence there's nothing to find. Review is bounded by what the reviewer actually checks — their familiarity with the code paths, how carefully they trace edge cases, how much time they had. A reviewer skimming a large diff under time pressure will pass code that a careful reader would flag. Silence tells you about the search, not the target.

Many real bugs don't show up by reading code at all: race conditions, off-by-one errors in rarely-hit branches, integration failures between components that each look fine in isolation, behavior that only breaks under specific data or load. Review is static — it reasons about what the code *should* do. Correctness is about what the code *actually* does when run. Those come apart constantly, which is why tests, staging, and production monitoring exist as separate layers, not redundant ones.

There's also a selection effect: the bugs most likely to survive review are exactly the ones review is bad at catching — subtle, non-local, or dependent on runtime state. A review passing cleanly can mean "the code is right" or it can mean "the bug here is invisible to static reading." From outside, those look identical. Treating a clean review as proof of correctness quietly biases you toward the second case, and by definition the survivors are the well-hidden ones.

Practically: treat an approved review as "no known objections from this reviewer, at this level of scrutiny," not "verified correct." Keep tests, monitoring, and runtime checks as independent evidence — they catch different failure classes, so absence of findings in one layer says nothing about the others.

This is why review pairs with tests, not replaces them: tests execute the code against real inputs and catch what static reading can't. A silent review plus a green test suite is real evidence; a silent review alone is just "nobody who looked happened to see it."

Reviewer blind spots compound this. A reviewer unfamiliar with a subsystem will miss violations of implicit invariants; a reviewer too familiar with the author's intent will read code as doing what it's supposed to do rather than what it actually does. Treat "no findings" as "no findings by this method, this reviewer, this time" — not as a correctness certificate. Pair review with tests, runtime verification, and monitoring; each catches failure modes the others structurally can't.

Keep writing tests for new code regardless of how clean it looked in review, and treat review as one layer in a stack — type checks, tests, code review, production monitoring — each catching a different class of failure the others miss.
